title: Someone uses guilt to get you to say yes
lede: A favour, a loan, a lift, a weekend, a commitment you do not have room for. When you hesitate, out comes the history: everything they have done for you, how little you call, how they would never have said no to you.

blocks.text: A favour, a loan, a lift, a weekend, a commitment you do not have room for. When you hesitate, out comes the history: everything they have done for you, how little you call, how they would never have said no to you.

items: Guilt is a legitimate emotion being used as a lever. The feeling is real; the obligation it implies is usually invented in the moment.
The request and the relationship are being deliberately fused, so that declining the request reads as rejecting the person. They are separable.
Speed favours the asker. Any answer given inside the emotional spike will be the answer they wanted.
Serial guilt-users are not tracking fairness. Saying yes does not reduce future demands; it recalibrates the baseline upward.

items.move: Do not answer inside the conversation
items.detail: Delay is the whole technique. "I will get back to you tonight" is a complete and reasonable response.

items.move: Separate the feeling from the decision
items.detail: Notice: I feel guilty, and this request is still unreasonable. Both can be entirely true.
Warmth on the relationship, clarity on the answer. Skipping the warmth makes it a fight; skipping the clarity makes it a negotiation.
One brief reason maximum. A list of reasons invites them to solve each one, and they will.

items.move: Offer a smaller real thing if you want to
items.detail: Only if you mean it. A grudging yes is worse for both of you than a clean no.
The second push is standard. Repeating your sentence unchanged is what teaches the boundary.

items.say: "I do not want to give you a rushed answer. Let me come back to you this evening."
"You have been generous with me and I remember it. I still cannot do this one."
"That is true, and I am grateful. It does not change my answer this time."
"I cannot do the weekend. I can do two hours on Saturday morning."

items: Inventing an elaborate excuse. It can be disproved and it makes you a liar in the next round.
Apologising three times. It signals the no is negotiable.
Counter-scorekeeping. Reciting your own past favours turns it into an audit nobody wins.
Saying yes and then withdrawing later. Far more expensive than a clean no now.
Notice whether the relationship survived. It almost always does, and that data is what makes the next no easier.
If there was punishment — silence, coldness, a campaign — that is information about the relationship, not about your decision.
Write down your standing limits: money you will lend, weekends you will give, notice you require. Pre-decided limits are much easier to hold.
Do one warm, unprompted thing for them later if you want the relationship. It decouples affection from compliance.
